Vukovar New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Vukovar, Croatia

Not demolished. Vukovar, first mentioned in 1231 at the Vuka-Danube confluence, became a multicultural trading hub after 150 years of Ottoman rule ended in 1687; by 1910 it counted 10,359 residents, mostly Croats, Germans, Serbs, and Hungarians. Ashkenazi Jews arrived from Austria in the early 19th century - just 27 by 1815 - organizing formally in 1837 with a prayer house (1841) and first synagogue (1876, later sold and converted to an Evangelical Church in 1910). A grand domed Central Synagogue, Croatia's first, opened in 1889, designed by Ludwig Schöne, alongside a Hebrew school for 20 pupils. Population peaked at 453 in 1921, falling to 213 by WWII. Despite generally warm relations with other residents - Jews were respected merchants and philanthropists - Croatian nationalists deported the entire community, including Rabbi Izrael Scheer and his wife, to Jasenovac, where all perished. Only 24 Jews remained by 1947; the Central Synagogue was sold to the municipality and demolished in 1958. This cemetery, established in 1850, holds tombstones from 1858 to 1948, in Hebrew, Hungarian, German, and Croatian; its 1928 Ceremonial Hall, one of the region's largest, combined Art Deco and Moorish elements before suffering heavy damage in the 1990s Croatian War of Independence, though it remains listed as Croatian Cultural Heritage.
